newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Q3 GDP - Review of expectations.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Q3 GDP - Review of expectations.

text.p: Australian gross domestic product (GDP) data for the September quarter will be released at 11.30 a.m. (0030 GMT).
The median forecast of the 29 economists Reuters surveyed is for quarterly growth a 0.9 percent, following on from the 0.1 percent growth in the June quarter.
In annual terms, growth is expected to moderate to around 3.4 percent from 4.5 percent in June, as the 2.0 percent growth posted in the September 1995 quarter drops out of calculations.
Forecasts for September quarter GDP growth range from 0.6 percent to 1.2 percent. September quarter forecasts, and previous data, are detailed below.
GDP (s/adj) Jun 95 Sep 95 Dec 95 Mar 96 Jun 96 Sep 96

Forecasts for the September quarter were revised upwards on Monday following the release of stronger than expected inventories data. Of the three measures of GDP, expenditure based GDP is expected to be the strongest, following on the strong inventories data, signs of strong capital expenditure, a reasonable contribution from private consumption and an expected strong contribution from net exports.

The fact that August employment was boosted by the inclusion of census workers should help income based GDP, as it is the mid month of each quarter that is used to calculate wages, salaries and supplements.

Production based GDP is the hardest component to forceast given the lack of partial indicators, but the fact that the Bureau of Statistics makes the annual erstminates for rural production in the September quarter should provide a solid base for this measure, economists said.

The slowing in annual growth will take GDP back to around 3.5 percent, a level many see as the economy's sustainable growth rate. While the economy is expected to remaion sluggish in the December quarter, many economists felt that in annual terms the second half of 1996 weould be the low point in economic growth for this part of the business cycle.

The September quarter should extend the unbroken run of uniterrupted economic growth to 21 quarters, but economists said there was a possibility that revisions to June quarter data contained in some of the partial indictors for the September quarter could turn that 0.1 percent rise into a fall.
As well as the headline growth figures, economists said they will be looking at the GDP data for updates on labour productivity and alternatiuve measures of inflation pressures

While the slowing in annual growth should be well received by financial markets looking for another rate cut, economists saw the September quarter data as having little impact on monetary policy decisions.

This is because not only is the data historical, but it will be affected by the uncertainty in the lead up to the August budget and will show only some of the very early effects of the first interest rate cut on July 31, they said.
